vignette: At forty-two, Elias has spent his adult life navigating North American coastlines, but three years ago the sea stops being his domain and becomes a crime scene. He stands at the helm of the MV Kestrel when a drifting container barge, its navigation lights dead and its crew asleep, slides into his starboard side. The impact tears through the hull like paper. He feels the sudden lurch, hears the shriek of tearing metal, smells diesel and salt flooding the bridge. He shouts orders that no one can hear over the groaning steel, then watches the main deck tilt thirty degrees in four minutes. The evacuation chime rings, a flat, mechanical tone that still plays in his sleep. When he wakes now, it’s not to an alarm but to the phantom vibration of engines beneath his ribs. He lies perfectly still, counting the seconds until his bedroom floor stops tilting. His wife, Mara, reaches for him, but he flinches before she even makes contact. He tells himself it’s just the sheets, but his chest tightens with a familiar, suffocating pressure. During the day, the world is full of triggers he once commanded without a second thought. A car backfiring on the way to the grocery store makes him slam the brakes. The hiss of the coffee maker sends his head snapping toward the ceiling. He stopped sailing six months after the incident. The coast guard clears the wreck, pays the claims, and assigns him an office job ashore, but he can’t bear the sight of any vessel on the horizon. He stares at the water from his porch until the light fades, his jaw clenched, waiting for a radio call that never comes. At home, Elias moves through the rooms like a ghost in his own life. He avoids the garage because the smell of gasoline reminds him of the spill. He won’t read about shipping routes, won’t even let his children draw boats. Mara asks him to talk, but the words feel lodged behind his sternum, heavy and sharp. He tells himself he’s protecting them, but he knows it’s easier to pull away than to admit he doesn’t know how to be safe anymore. He blames himself for the dead crew on the barge, for the oil that slicked the water, for surviving when two deckhands didn’t make it. The guilt isn’t a storm; it’s a slow leak, constant and unfixable. He drinks less now, not from discipline, but because the alcohol makes the edges of the world blur in a way that feels like drowning. In your office, he sits forward, hands resting on his knees, scanning the door, the windows, the fire extinguisher mounted on the wall. He answers your questions in short, precise sentences, the cadence of command habits still etched into his posture. When you ask about sleep, he looks at his watch, then away. “Four hours, maybe. The rest is just… static.” He talks about the way his shoulders ache from sleeping upright, how he jumps at the refrigerator’s compressor kicking on, how he checks the deadbolts three times before bed. He mentions Mara’s exhaustion, the quiet dinners, the way she used to trace his back but now rests her hand on the edge of the table instead. He doesn’t cry. He just exhales, a long, controlled breath, and watches the dust motes drift in the afternoon light. He is still standing at his post, waiting for an order that will tell him when it’s finally safe to let go.
